issues.item: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: The profile is centered on witnessed trauma with triggers involving crowded places, conversation topics, and bus riding, plus appraisals of vigilance and outsider status. The anger-loss-of-control appraisal introduces a distinct perpetration/impulse-control theme that is not supported by the other selected triggers, memory, threat, or strategy items, making it clinically hard to place within the same formulation.

Avoiding sex is not well linked to the rest of the profile. There are no sexual trauma cues, intimacy-related triggers, body-related appraisals, or threat/memory items that would explain sex-specific avoidance. Relative to the rest of the selected items, this strategy appears disconnected and inconsistent with the formulation.

vignette: As she sat in her quiet home office, surrounded by the familiar hum of computer equipment and the warm glow of screens, 72-year-old network engineer Rachel couldn't help but think back to that fateful day three years ago. She had been on a routine bus ride home from work when a violent altercation broke out between two passengers just a few seats away. The memory still played vividly in her mind - the shouting, the shattering of glass, and the blood-stained faces. In the aftermath of the incident, Rachel began to notice changes within herself. She started avoiding crowded places like shopping centers or public events, opting instead for quiet, solo activities at home. Her husband, Tom, grew concerned as she increasingly turned down social invitations, citing fatigue or not feeling up to it. But what frightened her most was the feeling of being constantly on edge - a nagging sense that something could go terribly wrong at any moment. Rachel started to limit her interactions with others, especially when conversation topics veered toward violence or trauma. She found herself mentally preparing for these discussions in advance, forcing a cheerful demeanor and focusing on "positive thoughts only." This coping strategy, though exhausting, helped her feel more in control. Yet, it also left her feeling disconnected from friends and family who didn't understand why she seemed so distant. As the months passed, Rachel's professional life began to suffer as well. She started taking longer routes to work to avoid certain bus lines or crowded areas, which sometimes made her late for meetings or deadlines. Her colleagues noticed a change in her behavior but attributed it to age-related stress or burnout. Meanwhile, Rachel became increasingly withdrawn from team projects and social gatherings at the office. Her thoughts were consumed by an unshakeable conviction that the world was a perilous place. She began to see potential threats everywhere - on public transport, in crowded areas, even in seemingly ordinary conversations. It was as if she had become a permanent outsider, watching life unfold from behind a veil of hypervigilance. Tom tried to reassure her that she was safe now, that the chances of another traumatic event were slim. But Rachel couldn't shake off the feeling of being on borrowed time. Her carefully constructed coping mechanisms - avoiding triggers and reframing negative thoughts - had become unsustainable. The weight of living in a constant state of alertness began to take its toll. The final straw came when Tom's 75th birthday celebration loomed, and Rachel found herself dreading the prospect of attending a crowded family gathering at their daughter's house. She knew she couldn't keep living like this - always fearful, always looking over her shoulder. The dread that had taken up residence in her chest was now suffocating her. Rachel finally agreed to seek professional help, acknowledging that she needed support to unravel the tangled web of thoughts and emotions that had become her reality. As she sat in the therapist's office, she hesitated, unsure what to expect but willing to confront the fears that had held her hostage for so long. For Rachel, this marked the first tentative step toward reentering a world that felt treacherous - and reclaiming her life from the grip of hypervigilance.
